Turkish baths work with kids — here's how to do it right

Taking children to a hammam is simpler than you'd think. Most accept kids from age 4 or 5 onward, though younger children can go if a parent stays with them the whole time. The key is choosing a family-friendly hammam, arriving early to avoid crowds, and explaining what happens beforehand so nothing surprises them.

posts.caption:
Istanbul hammams won't turn you away, but booking ahead saves hours of waiting.

Most hammams accept walk-ins, but popular ones in Sultanahmet and Beyoğlu fill up by mid-morning, especially on weekends. Book ahead online or by phone to guarantee entry at your chosen time—many offer English-language booking now. Walk-ins work best on weekday afternoons.

posts.caption:
How long should you spend in a hamam? 45 minutes to 2 hours.

Your first visit usually takes longer because staff explain each room and what happens next. A classic ritual moves you through three chambers: the cool room, the hot steam room, and the scrubbing room where a staff member exfoliates your skin. Regulars often skip straight to their favourite stage.

posts.caption:
A hammam visit takes 90 minutes but feels like stepping outside time.

You'll move through three rooms getting progressively hotter, lie on marble while someone scrubs your skin raw, then soak in cool water as your whole body unclenches. First-timers are always shocked how much dead skin comes off — bring a friend if you're nervous, go alone if you want to disappear.

posts.caption:
Cağaloğlu and Nuruosmaniye are ten minutes' walk apart in Fatih.

Both hammams date to the 1700s and both still run their original water systems. Cağaloğlu is the larger, with separate wings for men and women; Nuruosmaniye sits tucked behind its mosque and draws fewer tourists. Either takes 90 minutes from arrival to cool-down.
